lead: Hospitals, farms, sensor fleets and city offices all face the same problem: several parties keep separate databases, and each can quietly edit its own copy. The shared pattern is simple. A device or an organisation signs each piece of data. A small fingerprint of that data goes on a permissioned ledger. Applications then read one verifiable history. Health systems use it for records and consent, agriculture for crop provenance and payments, IoT for device identity and firmware logs, cities for parking, waste, energy and land records. The ledger stores fingerprints, not the raw data.
prereq: You need: Unit 2, Merkle trees and hash pointers, plus Chapter 6.2 on chaincode and endorsement.

sections.h3: Health: records, consent and clinical trials

blocks.text: A patient's history sits in many places: a hospital system, a lab, a pharmacy, an insurer. Each keeps its own database and each can edit it. A permissioned ledger fixes one narrow thing: who wrote which record, and when.
The ledger stores a hash of each record, not the record. A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint; changing the record changes the hash. The hospital keeps the full file off-chain.

Consent becomes a ledger entry. The patient signs a transaction saying: doctor X may read record hash H until 31 March. Chaincode checks the consent entry before releasing the file. Withdrawing consent writes a new entry, so the old grant stays in history — exactly what an audit needs.

Clinical trials use the same trick on documents. The protocol and each database lock (the frozen dataset at the end of a trial) are hashed and time-stamped when fixed, so a later change to a primary endpoint shows up as a broken link.

sections.h3: Off-chain data and on-chain Merkle roots

blocks.text: One vaccine fridge sends 6 readings per hour, so 144 per day. Thousands of fridges writing every reading would fill the ledger with numbers nobody reads again. So the gateway batches them.

items: The fridge reads the temperature and its device id, and the device signs the reading with its own private key; the gateway verifies that signature against the registered public key, then batches the signed readings.
It hashes each signed reading: hᵢ = SHA-256(reading).
It pairs the hashes and hashes again, level by level, until one root remains.
It sends one transaction: device id, date, root, and the number of readings in the batch.
To prove one reading, the app sends that reading plus its sibling hashes along the path; the verifier recomputes the root and compares it with the on-chain value.

blocks.where: n is the number of readings in one batch; ⌈ ⌉ rounds up, because the tree is padded to a power of two.

blocks.text: Raw readings stay in the hospital database: they are large, private, and a blockchain cannot delete a mistake.

Crop provenance is a chain of custody. Each step — farm, warehouse, mandi, packer, retailer — appends an event with quantity, date and a hash of its paperwork. The packet carries a QR code. A buyer scans it, sees the whole path, and knows that no event was inserted later.

Payments use chaincode escrow. The buyer's money is held by the contract and released when both sides sign the warehouse receipt. The farmer reads the condition in code instead of trusting a middleman's promise.

Field sensors add data: soil moisture, rainfall, a drone photo. These are hashed and batched like fridge readings. A crop-insurance payout can then follow a rainfall reading that farmer and insurer both verify, the same logic as the claims in Chapter 6.3.

A device needs an identity before its data means anything. Each device gets a key pair; its public key is registered against a manufacturer and an approved firmware hash. A gateway rejects readings signed by an unknown key, or by a device whose firmware hash is not on the list. Firmware updates are logged as transactions, so an owner can prove which version a meter ran on a given date.

items: Parking: the sensor records the spot as free, the ledger records the release and the payment, so the driver cannot dispute a signed record.
Waste: bins report fill level, collection trips are logged, and the contractor is paid per verified trip.
Smart grid: smart meters send signed readings; a neighbourhood micro-grid trades surplus solar units, and the ledger settles who sent what.
E-governance: land records and licences are stored as hashes, so the citizen holds a copy that any office can check.

figure.caption: All 144 readings stay in the hospital database; only one 32-byte Merkle root goes on the ledger, so an auditor checks a single reading with 8 sibling hashes instead of all 144. Three readings above 8 °C are 2.08% of the day.

spec.title: One fridge, one day: 144 readings → 1 root
spec.aria: A vaccine fridge sends 6 readings per hour (144 a day) to an IoT gateway, which builds a Merkle tree and writes one 32-byte root to the blockchain while keeping the raw readings in the hospital database; an auditor checks one reading with 8 sibling hashes.

examples.question: A vaccine fridge sends one temperature reading every 10 minutes. (a) How many readings does it produce in a day? (b) The gateway writes one Merkle root per day. How many sibling hashes does a proof for one reading need at most? (c) Three readings are above 8 °C. What percentage of the day's readings is that, to two decimals?
steps: Find the smallest k with 2^k ≥ 144: 2⁷ = 128 is too small, 2⁸ = 256 is enough, so k = 8.
Proof length = ⌈log₂ 144⌉ = 8 sibling hashes; each level of the tree adds one hash.
Storage: all 144 readings stay in the hospital database; the chain gets one 32-byte root.
examples.answer: (a) 144 readings per day, (b) at most 8 sibling hashes, (c) 2.08 % of the readings are above 8 °C.
examples.check:
import math
per_hour = 60 // 10
per_day = per_hour * 24
proof = math.ceil(math.log2(per_day))
pct = round(3 / per_day * 100, 2)
print(per_day)
print(proof)
print(pct)

traps: Putting raw IoT readings on-chain. Keep the raw readings in the hospital database and put only a hash or a Merkle root on the ledger, so the ledger stays small.
Believing the ledger proves the reading was correct. It proves the reading was not changed after it was written, not that the sensor was calibrated.
Mixing up the root and the proof. The root is one hash on the ledger; the proof is the short list of sibling hashes.
Using n instead of ⌈log₂ n⌉ for proof length. For 144 readings the proof is 8 hashes, not 144.
Expecting consent to be erased. Revocation is a new entry; the old grant stays visible in history.

quiz.q: What does the ledger store for a patient record kept off-chain?
quiz.a: A hash (fingerprint) of the record, plus the writer's identity and a timestamp.

quiz.q: Why does the gateway batch a day of readings into one Merkle root instead of writing each reading?
quiz.a: Volume and privacy. One root per batch keeps the ledger small and keeps the raw readings in the hospital database.

quiz.q: A fridge sends 96 readings per day, batched into one Merkle tree. How many sibling hashes does one proof need at most?
quiz.a: Smallest k with 2^k ≥ 96: 2⁶ = 64 is too small, 2⁷ = 128 is enough, so 7 sibling hashes.

quiz.q: How does a firmware hash on the ledger help an auditor after a meter misreads?
quiz.a: The auditor sees which firmware version the meter was running on that date. If the hash is not on the approved list, the misreading is explained without guessing.

quiz.q: Name two smart-city services and say what the ledger records for each.
quiz.a: Parking (spot released and payment) and waste collection (trips done, payment released). Energy metering and land records are also valid.

quiz.q: Why does withdrawing consent not delete the earlier consent entry?
quiz.a: The ledger is append-only. A revocation is a new entry, and the old grant must stay visible so an audit can see who had access and when.

quiz.q: Farmer and insurer dispute a rainfall reading. How does a Merkle proof settle it?
quiz.a: Both take the reading and its sibling hashes from the day's batch. Each recomputes upward to the root. If the result equals the root already on the ledger, the reading is the one that was committed, and neither side can alter it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is moving consent and device identity towards verifiable credentials and decentralised identifiers, where the holder carries a signed claim instead of asking an office to confirm it. Agri-food traceability is converging on event standards such as GS1 EPCIS, with hashes of those events on a ledger. Energy pilots study peer-to-peer solar trading settled on a ledger. Search next for verifiable credentials, DIDs, EPCIS, and energy web platforms.
